issues.legal_issue: A court may order restoration of a co-owner’s separate possession during a pending partition suit when the parties had mutually arranged separate occupation and another co-owner forcibly changed that possession.
material_facts: The parties were co-owners in a pending partition suit and had entered into a development agreement under which separate flats were allotted for their occupation.
The plaintiffs had earlier stated that the parties were in possession of separate flats by mutual adjustment, and the first respondent was in possession of the flat at issue.
The plaintiffs later put a padlock on that flat and obstructed the first respondent’s use of it during the proceedings.

The trial court found on the material before it that the first respondent had been in possession and that the plaintiffs had put the padlock and household articles in the flat; it directed their removal and restrained further obstruction.
issues.conclusion: The mandatory injunction directing removal of the padlock and articles and preventing further obstruction was lawful. The appeal was dismissed, and the order was not disturbed.
issues.legal_principle: Possession of one co-owner is generally treated as possession of all, but that principle does not prevent co-owners from separately occupying property under a mutual arrangement, and a co-owner may not forcibly dispossess another in breach of that arrangement. A court may use its inherent power under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to grant an injunction where the matter is not covered by Order 39, Rules 1 and 2. If a party changes possession by force during a suit, the court may restore the prior position; a person entitled to prohibitory relief may also be entitled to mandatory relief. The Court relied on Manohar Lal Chopra v. Rai Bahadur Rao Raja Seth Hiralal and India Household and Healthcare Ltd. v. LG Household and Healthcare Ltd. on inherent power; Israil v. Samset Rahman and Spandan Diagnostic & Research Centre Private Limited v. Shri Ritendra Nath Ghosh on injunction protecting a co-owner in exclusive possession; and Jahuri Sah v. Dwarika Prasad Jhunjhunwala on arrangements between co-owners for enjoyment of undivided property. It distinguished Mohammad Baqar v. Naim-un-Nisa Bibi, Bhaguji Bayaji Pokale v. Kantilal Baban Gunjawate, Abu Shahid v. Abdul Hoque Dobhash, Hemanta Kumar Banerjee v. Satish Chandra Banerjee, and Kishore Kumar Khaitan v. Praveen Kumar Singh because they did not displace the result on the facts established here.

predicates.partition_suit_pending: The parties were litigating a claim to partition jointly owned property.
predicates.coowners_mutually_arranged_separate_occu: The co-owners had agreed to occupy separate parts of the jointly owned property.
predicates.prior_possession_supported_by_record: The record, including the parties’ statements or other material, supported that the person seeking relief had occupied the disputed part before the change.
predicates.another_coowner_forcibly_changed_possess: Another co-owner obstructed that occupation or changed the possession by force during the proceeding.

issues.definition: When a partition suit is pending, the co-owners arranged separate occupation, the prior occupation is supported by the record, and another co-owner forcibly changes it, the court may restore the prior possession by mandatory injunction.
